claims.text: The baseline tungsten-, niobium-, and molybdenum-rich refractory high-entropy alloy is optimized for high-temperature performance but limited by high density.
Adding 1–3 at.% aluminum will induce a fine-scale B2-ordered precipitate phase.
The B2 precipitates will be nanoscale and uniformly distributed within the alloy matrix.
The B2 precipitates will obstruct dislocation motion at high temperature.
Precipitation strengthening from the B2 phase will increase high-temperature yield strength.
Precipitation strengthening from the B2 phase will improve creep resistance.
Aluminum addition will reduce the alloy's overall density because aluminum is a lighter element.
A low B2 precipitate volume fraction will prevent significant loss of room-temperature ductility.
The aluminum-modified alloy will retain similar room-temperature mechanical performance to the aluminum-free baseline.
The aluminum-modified alloy will exhibit approximately 20–30% greater high-temperature yield strength than the baseline.
The aluminum-modified alloy will have approximately 5–10% lower density than the baseline.
The proposed benefits will hold under mechanical loading at approximately 800–1000°C.
Approximately 800–1000°C and the proposed loading conditions are typical of jet-turbine operation.
The beneficial effects occur only within a narrow aluminum concentration window.
Excess aluminum could produce coarse or high-volume-fraction precipitates.
Coarse or high-volume-fraction precipitates could embrittle the alloy at room temperature or impair high-temperature performance.
